segments.html:
Introduction

A linear probe tells us that some concept — the gender of a name, the sentiment of a review, the language of a sentence — is linearly decodable from a model's residual stream. It does not tell us that the model uses it. Concept erasure is the intervention that turns the correlational claim into a causal one: we remove the concept's linear subspace from the residual stream, let the rest of the network run on the erased state, and watch what breaks.

Two methods are standard, and we run both:

  • LEACE (Least-squares Concept Erasure, Belrose et al., 2023) computes the minimal affine edit under which no linear probe beats chance. For a binary concept it is rank 1, and it comes with a guarantee.
  • INLP (Iterative Nullspace Projection, Ravfogel et al., 2020) repeatedly trains a probe and projects out its weight vector. It has no optimality guarantee, but it produces a nested family of projections — one fit gives you every rank — so it is the method that can answer "how many directions does this concept need?"

The part that makes this an nnsight tutorial rather than a scikit-learn one is where the projection is applied. Fitting an eraser on saved activations and multiplying the saved tensor by it proves nothing about the model: the forward pass already happened, the logits were already produced from the unerased state. To make a causal claim we have to apply the projection inside the forward pass, so that every downstream layer, and the unembedding, only ever see erased activations. In nnsight that is two lines inside a trace:

segments.code:
h = model.transformer.h[6].output
model.transformer.h[6].output = mu + (h - mu) @ M

segments.html:
Over the course of the notebook we hold ourselves to four standards, each of which is a step most write-ups skip:

  1. The probe is real. A shuffled-label control sits at chance, and the concept is not leaking through sequence length or position.
  2. The concept dies for a probe retrained on the erased activations, not merely for the probe we already had. Any projection defeats its own probe; that is not evidence of anything.
  3. An unrelated capability survives, and the comparison is against a rank-matched random projection. Deleting directions always costs something; the question is whether a learned direction buys more erasure per unit of damage than an arbitrary one.
  4. Erasing at one layer is not enough. Later layers rebuild the concept, and we show the refill.

We use gpt2 throughout, so the whole notebook runs in a few minutes on a single small GPU.

segments.html:
The concept: gender of a first name

We need a concept that GPT-2 genuinely represents and visibly uses, so that erasing it has something to break. Gender of an English first name is a good choice: a probe reads it easily from the residual stream, and the model's use of it is observable at the logits — after "Yesterday Sarah went to the store because" GPT-2 prefers " she" over " he", and the preference flips for a male name. That gives us a decoding measure and a behavioural measure of the same concept.

The dataset is 88 male and 88 female first names crossed with 12 sentence templates.

segments.html:
Two details in the templates are load-bearing, and both exist to stop the label leaking through something other than the model's representation of gender.

⚠️ Keep only names that are a single token with a leading space. GPT-2's tokenizer splits female first names into more pieces than male ones on average, so a mixed set makes sequences of different lengths for the two classes. Sequence length changes the positional embeddings and the index of the last real token, and a probe will happily read gender off that instead. It will not error; it will just give you a suspiciously high number at layer 0.

⚠️ The name is never sentence-initial. Every template starts with a filler word, so within one template every sequence has the same length and the same token at every position except the name.

We split by name, not by sentence: the 28 test names never appear in training. A split by sentence would let the probe memorise names rather than learn the concept.

def build_set(names_m, names_f, templates=TEMPLATES):

segments.html:
Step 1: A probe for the concept

Erasure needs a direction, and a direction comes from a probe. We train an L2-regularised logistic regression on the residual stream — the output of a transformer block — and report it two ways:

  • all positions: every non-pad token of every sequence is a training example. This is the distribution we will fit the erasers on.
  • last token: only the final token of each sequence, which is the position the model actually predicts from.

Keep the distinction in mind; in the caveats we will find that it matters a great deal.

To collect activations we use tracer.cache. Three rules, all of which we rely on later:

  • Always pass modules=. An unfiltered tracer.cache() records every module in the tree — about 150 of them for GPT-2 — and copies them all to the host synchronously. That is the difference between a three-second collection and a five-minute one.
  • Declare the cache as the first statement in the trace body, before any .output read or assignment. This is the opposite of the forward-pass ordering rule that governs everything else, and skipping it raises ValueError: tracer.cache() must be declared before reading or modifying a model value. The cache still records post-intervention values — that is exactly what we need in Step 4.
  • Wrap read-only collection in torch.no_grad(). A trace runs with autograd on by default, which costs a lot of memory for nothing when we are only reading.

The helper below already takes an erasers argument. We pass None for now; apply_erasure is defined in Step 3.
Because we pool over token positions, we need to know which sequence (and therefore which label) each row of the stacked activation matrix came from, and which rows are final tokens.

segments.text: 20880 train token positions, 9744 test token positions

segments.html: The probe itself is a full-batch LBFGS logistic regression on the GPU. sklearn's LogisticRegression gives the same answer (we check that below), but we will fit this probe dozens of times during the rank sweep and the GPU version keeps the notebook to a few minutes.

segments.code:
def probe_accuracy(X_train, y_tr, X_test, y_te, l2=1e-3, steps=150):
    """L2 logistic regression, standardised with the train statistics. Returns test accuracy."""
    X_train = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(X_train)).float().to(DEVICE)
    X_test  = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(X_test)).float().to(DEVICE)
    y_tr_t  = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(y_tr)).float().to(DEVICE)
    y_te_t  = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(y_te)).float().to(DEVICE)

    mu, sd = X_train.mean(0, True), X_train.std(0, True).clamp(min=1e-6)
    X_train, X_test = (X_train - mu) / sd, (X_test - mu) / sd

    w = torch.zeros(X_train.shape[1], device=DEVICE, requires_grad=True)
    b = torch.zeros(1, device=DEVICE, requires_grad=True)
    opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([w, b], max_iter=steps, history_size=20, tolerance_grad=1e-9,
                            tolerance_change=1e-12, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe")
    loss_fn = torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()

    def closure():
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(X_train @ w + b, y_tr_t) + l2 * (w * w).sum()
        loss.backward()
        return loss

    opt.step(closure)
    with torch.no_grad():
        return float((((X_test @ w + b) > 0).float() == y_te_t).float().mean())

Gender is strongly decodable everywhere, and the two readings differ: pooled over all token positions the probe sits around 0.91–0.93, while at the final token it reaches 0.98–1.00 in the upper blocks. That is the expected shape — the name token carries the concept from the start, and by the last position the model has gathered it in order to predict a pronoun.

Before we trust any of that, two controls. A probe accuracy is only meaningful next to the number the same pipeline produces when there is nothing to find.

  • Shuffled labels. Refit the block-6 probe with the training labels permuted. If this is not at chance, the probe is fitting something structural about the pipeline, not the concept.
  • The embedding layer. transformer.drop is the residual stream before block 0 — token plus positional embeddings and nothing else. Within a template every sequence has an identical final token at an identical index, so a last-token probe there must be exactly at chance. If it is not, sequence length is leaking the label, which is the trap the single-token filter was built to avoid.

We also check our GPU probe against sklearn, so that a wrong number cannot be blamed on the optimiser.

segments.code:
def collect_embeddings(texts, batch_size=128):
    out = []
    for start in range(0, len(texts), batch_size):
        input_ids, attn_mask = tokenize(texts[start:start + batch_size])
        with torch.no_grad(), model.trace(input_ids, attention_mask=attn_mask) as tracer:
            cache = tracer.cache(modules=[model.transformer.drop],
                                 device=torch.device("cpu"), dtype=torch.float32)
        out.append(cache["model.transformer.drop"].output[attn_mask.cpu().bool()].half())
    return torch.cat(out)

emb_train, emb_test = collect_embeddings(train_texts), collect_embeddings(test_texts)

y_shuffled = np.random.RandomState(0).permutation(y_train)
shuffled_acc = probe_accuracy(base_train[6], y_shuffled, base_test[6], y_test)
embed_acc = probe_accuracy(emb_train[TRAIN_LAST], y_train[TRAIN_LAST],
                           emb_test[TEST_LAST],   y_test[TEST_LAST])

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
Xtr = base_train[11][TRAIN_LAST].float().numpy()
Xte = base_test[11][TEST_LAST].float().numpy()
scaler = StandardScaler().fit(Xtr)
sk = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(scaler.transform(Xtr), y_train[TRAIN_LAST])
sk_acc = sk.score(scaler.transform(Xte), y_test[TEST_LAST])

print(f"gender probe, block 6, all positions          : {acc_all[6]:.3f}")
print(f"shuffled-label control, block 6               : {shuffled_acc:.3f}")
print(f"embedding layer, last token (must be chance)  : {embed_acc:.3f}")
print(f"block 11 last token, ours vs sklearn          : {acc_last[11]:.3f} vs {sk_acc:.3f}")

The shuffled-label probe is at chance and the embedding-layer probe is at exactly 0.500, so nothing in the pipeline leaks the label and every point in the plot above is carried there by attention. Our probe and sklearn's agree to three decimals. The wiring is anchored; we can start erasing.

Step 2: Fitting the erasers

All three erasers we use are affine maps of the same shape,

x↦μ+(x−μ)M,

where μ is the mean activation at the site and M is a d×d matrix. Writing it this way keeps the mean of the distribution fixed and only removes variance along the erased directions, which is what makes the edit small.

LEACE picks the smallest such map (in the least-squares sense) that makes the concept linearly unpredictable. Working in the whitened space W=Σxx−1/2​, it projects out the direction of the whitened cross-covariance Σxz​. For a binary label Σxz​ is a single vector, so LEACE is rank 1 and there is no rank knob to turn.

segments.code:
def _sym_inv_sqrt(S, tol=1e-8):
    evals, U = torch.linalg.eigh(S)
    evals = evals.clamp(min=0)
    keep = evals > tol * evals.max()
    inv  = torch.where(keep, evals.clamp(min=1e-30).rsqrt(), torch.zeros_like(evals))
    root = torch.where(keep, evals.sqrt(), torch.zeros_like(evals))
    return (U * inv) @ U.T, (U * root) @ U.T          # Sigma^-1/2, Sigma^+1/2


def fit_leace(X, z):
    """LEACE (Belrose et al. 2023). Returns (M, mu) for x -> mu + (x - mu) @ M."""
    X = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(X)).double()
    z = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(z)).double()
    N, d = X.shape

    mu = X.mean(0)
    Xc = X - mu
    zc = (z - z.mean()).unsqueeze(1)

    sigma_xx = (Xc.T @ Xc) / (N - 1)
    sigma_xz = (Xc.T @ zc) / (N - 1)

    W, W_pinv = _sym_inv_sqrt(sigma_xx)
    B = W @ sigma_xz
    B = B / B.norm()
    A = W_pinv @ (B @ B.T) @ W                        # the rank-1 correction
    return torch.eye(d, dtype=torch.float64) - A.T, mu

segments.html:
INLP is the loop: fit a linear probe on the data projected into the current nullspace, take its weight vector, orthogonalise it against the directions already removed, and append it to an orthonormal basis Q. The rank-k eraser is then the orthogonal projection Pk​=I−Q:k​Q:k⊤​. Because Q is nested, one fit gives us every rank at once.

The random rank-k eraser is the control: the same I−QQ⊤ with a random orthonormal Q. It removes exactly as many directions, so any difference between the two is attributable to which directions, not how many.

segments.code:
def _logreg_direction(X, y, l2=1e-5, steps=200):
    X = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(X)).float().to(DEVICE)
    y = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(y)).float().to(DEVICE)
    Xs = (X - X.mean(0, True)) / X.std().clamp(min=1e-6)

    w = torch.zeros(X.shape[1], device=DEVICE, requires_grad=True)
    b = torch.zeros(1, device=DEVICE, requires_grad=True)
    opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([w, b], max_iter=steps, history_size=20, tolerance_grad=1e-9,
                            tolerance_change=1e-12, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe")
    loss_fn = torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()

    def closure():
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_fn(Xs @ w + b, y) + l2 * (w * w).sum()
        loss.backward()
        return loss

    opt.step(closure)
    with torch.no_grad():
        train_acc = float((((Xs @ w + b) > 0).float() == y).float().mean())
    return w.detach().double().cpu(), train_acc


def fit_inlp(X, z, k):
    """INLP (Ravfogel et al. 2020). Returns (Q [d, k] orthonormal, mu, per-iteration train accuracy)."""
    X = torch.as_tensor(np.asarray(X)).double()
    d = X.shape[1]
    mu = X.mean(0)
    Xc = X - mu
    Q = torch.zeros(d, 0, dtype=torch.float64)
    accs = []
    for _ in range(k):
        P = torch.eye(d, dtype=torch.float64) - Q @ Q.T
        w, acc = _logreg_direction((Xc @ P).float(), z)
        accs.append(acc)
        w = w - Q @ (Q.T @ w)                          # orthogonalise against what we removed
        if w.norm() < 1e-9:
            break
        Q = torch.cat([Q, (w / w.norm()).unsqueeze(1)], dim=1)
    return Q, mu, accs


def projection(Q, k):
    Qk = Q[:, :k]
    return torch.eye(Q.shape[0], dtype=torch.float64) - Qk @ Qk.T


def random_basis(d, k, seed=0):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    Q, _ = torch.linalg.qr(torch.randn(d, k, generator=g, dtype=torch.float64))
    return Q

segments.html:
We erase at block 6 and every block above it. Step 5 shows why a single block is not enough. Every eraser is fitted per site, on that site's own training-name activations, using all token positions.

⚠️ Fit the erasers on the training names only. An eraser fitted on the test names would be told the answer, and the held-out probe accuracy afterwards would mean nothing.

segments.code:
LAYER = 6
SITES = list(range(LAYER, N_LAYERS))
K_MAX = 12

leace, inlp_Q, rand_Q, site_mu, inlp_train_acc = {}, {}, {}, {}, {}
for site in SITES:
    X = base_train[site].float()
    site_mu[site] = X.double().mean(0)
    leace[site] = fit_leace(X, y_train)
    inlp_Q[site], _, inlp_train_acc[site] = fit_inlp(X, y_train, K_MAX)
    rand_Q[site] = random_basis(D_MODEL, K_MAX, seed=100 + site)

print("erasure sites:", SITES)
print("INLP per-iteration train accuracy at block 6:",
      " ".join(f"{a:.3f}" for a in inlp_train_acc[LAYER]))

segments.html: The INLP trace is worth reading on its own: the first direction takes a training probe from 0.92 to 0.70, the next few shave off a little more, and from the sixth onwards it sits in a flat tail at 0.52–0.56, where the "directions" INLP returns are increasingly fit to noise. That flattening is the first hint of where the useful rank ends — we measure it properly in Step 7. It is also why we stop at rank 12: past the point where the iteration accuracy stops moving, INLP keeps deleting directions that no longer carry the concept but still carry everything else.

Step 3: Erasing inside the forward pass

Here is the distinction the whole tutorial turns on.

If we take the activations we cached above, multiply them by M, and retrain a probe, we learn exactly one thing: that our projection defeats a linear probe on a matrix of numbers. The model never saw those numbers. Its logits were computed from the unerased state; blocks 7 to 11 read the unerased state; the prediction of " she" after "Sarah" is untouched. A post-hoc projection cannot say anything about what the model does, because by the time it is applied the model has already done it.

An in-pass erasure replaces the block's output while the forward pass is still running, so every downstream module — every later block, the final layer norm, the unembedding — consumes the erased tensor. That is a causal intervention, and it is what lets us ask whether the concept was used.

In nnsight the intervention is an assignment to .output inside a trace:

segments.code:
def apply_erasure(erasers):
    """Apply x -> mu + (x - mu) @ M to each site's block output, at every token position."""
    for site in sorted(erasers):                # forward-pass order
        M, mu = erasers[site]
        h = blocks[site].output                 # a bare (batch, seq, d_model) tensor
        blocks[site].output = mu + (h - mu) @ M

segments.html:
⚠️ A decoder block's .output in current transformers is a plain tensor, not a tuple. Writing blocks[site].output[0] selects batch row 0 — it raises no error and silently erases one sequence out of the batch. (The attention submodule, blocks[site].attn, does return a tuple. When unsure, check with isinstance(module.output, tuple).)

⚠️ M must have the model's dtype. Assigning a float32 matrix into a bfloat16 model does not fail at the assignment; it fails several modules later inside F.linear, with a traceback that mentions neither nnsight nor the module you assigned to. to_device above casts for us.

Note the sites are iterated in sorted order. Within one invoke, nnsight requires modules to be requested in the order they execute; asking for block 9 and then block 7 deadlocks and raises OutOfOrderError.

Let's see the intervention do something. We run the same two prompts twice in a single forward pass using tracer.invoke: one invoke untouched, one with the eraser installed at blocks 6–11. Batching this way rather than looping over two traces is the idiomatic nnsight move — the two conditions are separate rows of one batch, and an intervention inside one invoke only touches that invoke's rows.

    with tracer.invoke(demo_prompts):
        clean_logits = model.lm_head.output[:, -1].save()
    with tracer.invoke(demo_prompts):

        erased_logits = model.lm_head.output[:, -1].save()

Step 4: The anchor — a probe retrained on the erased activations

This is the step most write-ups get wrong. After applying a projection P it is trivially true that the original probe, whose weight vector w satisfies Pw≈0, no longer works. That is arithmetic, not evidence. The question is whether the concept is still there for any linear probe — so we retrain the probe from scratch on activations collected with the erasure running, and evaluate it on held-out names.

We compare four conditions at block 6: no erasure, LEACE (rank 1), INLP at rank 12, and a rank-matched random projection at rank 12.

segments.code:
def decodability(erasers, layers, last_token_too=True):
    acts_tr, _ = collect(train_texts, erasers=erasers, layers=layers)
    acts_te, _ = collect(test_texts,  erasers=erasers, layers=layers)
    pooled = {l: probe_accuracy(acts_tr[l], y_train, acts_te[l], y_test) for l in layers}
    last = {l: probe_accuracy(acts_tr[l][TRAIN_LAST], y_train[TRAIN_LAST],
                              acts_te[l][TEST_LAST],  y_test[TEST_LAST]) for l in layers} \
           if last_token_too else {}
    return pooled, last

Step 5: Notch and refill

Erasing at a single block is the natural first thing to try, and it does not do what one hopes. A transformer's residual stream is written to by every layer; if the information that lets a later block recompute the concept survives anywhere — in an earlier block's contribution, in a nonlinear residue — the later blocks will put the direction back.

We measure this directly: retrain a probe at every block, under three conditions — no erasure, LEACE at block 6 only, and LEACE at every block from 6 to 11.

Erasing at block 6 alone produces a single sharp notch: the probe drops to 0.533 at block 6 and is back to 0.819 one block later, climbing to 0.874 by block 11. One layer of computation is enough for the model to rebuild a linearly decodable gender direction, which is why any claim of the form "we removed gender at layer L" needs to say what happened at layer L+1. The next section measures the behavioural consequence: erasing at block 6 alone takes gendered-pronoun accuracy from 0.993 only as far as 0.828, while the same eraser applied at all six blocks takes it to 0.562.

Erasing at every block from 6 upward keeps decodability lower everywhere downstream, though not at chance — around 0.81. That residual is itself informative, and we return to it in the caveats.

Step 6: Collateral damage, and the control that matters

Any projection removes capacity. A rank-12 erasure deletes 12 of 768 directions from the residual stream at six layers, and something will get worse. The scientific question is not "did erasure cost anything" — it always does — but whether a learned direction buys more erasure per unit of damage than an arbitrary one. So every erasure below is reported next to a random projection of the same rank at the same sites.

We measure three unrelated things and one related one:

  • Perplexity on 96 x 128 tokens of wikitext-103 validation — general language modelling.
  • Subject–verb agreement over 288 minimal pairs ("The key near the tables" → " is" vs "The keys near the table" → " are") — a specific syntactic capability that has nothing to do with gender.
  • An unrelated concept probe at the erased block: animal vs vehicle nouns. If erasure is specific, another linearly decodable concept at the same site should survive.
  • Behaviour: on 448 held-out-name prompts, does logit(" he") - logit(" she") still have the sign the name implies?

import datasets

wikitext = datasets.load_dataset("Salesforce/wikitext", "wikitext-103-raw-v1", split="validation")
ppl_tokens = tokenizer("\n".join(t for t in wikitext["text"] if len(t) > 200),
                       return_tensors="pt").input_ids[0]
N_CHUNK, CHUNK_LEN = 96, 128
ppl_ids = ppl_tokens[:N_CHUNK * CHUNK_LEN].view(N_CHUNK, CHUNK_LEN).to(DEVICE)
clear_output()

def perplexity(erasers):
    total_nll, n_tok = 0.0, 0
    for start in range(0, N_CHUNK, 16):
        ids = ppl_ids[start:start + 16]
        with torch.no_grad(), model.trace(ids):
            if erasers:
                apply_erasure(erasers)
            logits = model.lm_head.output.save()
        logprobs = torch.log_softmax(logits[:, :-1].float(), -1)
        targets = ids[:, 1:]
        total_nll += float(-logprobs.gather(-1, targets.unsqueeze(-1)).sum())
        n_tok += targets.numel()
    return float(np.exp(total_nll / n_tok))

# --- subject-verb agreement -------------------------------------------------
NOUNS = ["key", "book", "lamp", "chair", "bottle", "window", "phone", "plate", "clock",
         "box", "card", "door", "rope", "shirt", "wheel", "tool", "brush", "coin"]
DISTRACTORS = ["table", "cabinet", "garden", "office", "kitchen", "shelf", "corner", "station"]
agr_texts, agr_is_plural = [], []
for noun in NOUNS:
    for other in DISTRACTORS:
        agr_texts.append(f"The {noun} near the {other}s");  agr_is_plural.append(0)
        agr_texts.append(f"The {noun}s near the {other}");  agr_is_plural.append(1)
agr_is_plural = np.array(agr_is_plural)
is_id, are_id = tokenizer.encode(" is")[0], tokenizer.encode(" are")[0]

def agreement(erasers):
    _, logits = collect(agr_texts, erasers=erasers)
    predicted_plural = (logits[:, are_id] > logits[:, is_id]).numpy().astype(int)
    return float((predicted_plural == agr_is_plural).mean())

spec_test_texts,  spec_test_y  = build_set(ANIMALS[10:], VEHICLES[10:], NOUN_TEMPLATES)

def evaluate(name, erasers):
    if name in RESULTS:
        return RESULTS[name]
    pooled, _ = decodability(erasers, [LAYER], last_token_too=False)

The LEACE r=1, block 6 only row is the other half of Step 5. That eraser drives block-6 decodability to exactly the same 0.533 as the six-site version and costs almost exactly the same perplexity (+11.9% vs +12.1%), yet behaviour only falls to 0.828 instead of 0.562: the model rebuilds the direction in blocks 7–11 and goes on using it. Erasure has to be applied at every block above the site to hold, and the cost of doing so is close to free once you have paid for the first site.

The specificity controls hold. Subject–verb agreement is 1.000 under every INLP erasure we ran, and under LEACE — the model still tracks number through a distractor noun. The random projections, which are supposed to be the harmless comparison, are the ones that start dropping agreement (0.986 at rank 4, 0.951 at rank 12). The unrelated animal/vehicle probe at the erased block reads 0.864 against a baseline of 0.864: another linearly decodable concept, at the same site, at the same time, is completely untouched. The erasure is removing gender, not degrading block 6.

One asymmetry is worth naming: LEACE rank 1 is the most expensive intervention per direction removed (+12.1% perplexity for a single direction, more than INLP at rank 12). LEACE's projection is oblique — it is orthogonal in the whitened metric, not in the activation metric — so its operator norm on the raw residual stream is large. If you care about collateral damage rather than the formal guarantee, INLP's orthogonal projections are the better buy.

Behaviour dies first. The rightmost panel is at chance by rank 4 (0.556) and does not improve with more directions — in fact it drifts slightly up again at higher rank. Four directions out of 768, at six blocks, are enough to sever the connection between a name and its pronoun.

The knee is at rank 4. Past it we buy about 0.07 of decodability for three times the perplexity cost and no further behavioural change.

Erasure that persists: generation under an edit

Everything so far has been one trace at a time. To watch the model generate under erasure we install the intervention as a persistent edit with model.edit(inplace=True), which stores the intervention on the envoy and replays it on every subsequent trace or generate call. The body goes under for _ in tracer.iter[:] so that it re-applies at every decoding step, not just the first.

segments.code:
def generate(prompts, max_new_tokens=12):
    out = []
    for p in prompts:
        with torch.no_grad(), model.generate(p, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens, do_sample=False,
                                             pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id) as tracer:
            tokens = tracer.result.save()
        out.append(tokenizer.decode(tokens[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
    return out

gen_prompts = ["Yesterday Sarah went to the store because",
               "Apparently Daniel was very tired, so",
               "The manager thanked Jessica because"]

baseline_gen = generate(gen_prompts)

with model.edit(inplace=True) as tracer:
    for _ in tracer.iter[:]:
        apply_erasure(erasers_all)

erased_gen = generate(gen_prompts)

model.clear_edits()
restored_gen = generate(gen_prompts)

for p, b, e in zip(gen_prompts, baseline_gen, erased_gen):
    print(f"baseline: {b}")
    print(f"erased  : {e}\n")
print("clear_edits() restored the baseline generations exactly:", restored_gen == baseline_gen)

LEACE or INLP?

Having run both, the choice is not arbitrary:

  • LEACE when you want the guarantee. It is the provably minimal affine edit under which no linear probe beats chance on the fitted distribution, it needs no probe training and no hyperparameters, and for a binary concept it is a single direction. Its costs: rank 1 is all you get (so it cannot answer rank questions), and its oblique projection is surprisingly expensive on the raw residual stream — +12.1% perplexity here, more than INLP at rank 12.
  • INLP when you want the rank family. One fit gives every rank, so the sweep in Step 7 is possible at all; its projections are orthogonal and therefore cheap; and its per-iteration accuracy is a free diagnostic of how much concept is left. Its costs: no guarantee, a probe (and its hyperparameters) inside the loop, and directions past the knee that are fit to noise.

In practice: use LEACE to make the claim, INLP to find the operating point.

Caveats

The eraser only erases on the distribution it was fitted on

The last-token column in Step 4 barely moved, and that is not an accident of our code. LEACE's guarantee is that no linear probe beats chance on the distribution the eraser was fitted on — and we fitted on activations pooled over all token positions. Restricted to the final-token sub-population, gender is still ~97% decodable.

We can test this directly: refit the same LEACE at the same block on last-token activations only, apply it at every position as before, and see which slice goes to chance.

The numbers swap. Each eraser drives its own distribution to chance and does almost nothing to the other, and the cosine similarity between the two rank-1 corrections is 0.144 — the pooled "gender direction" and the final-token "gender direction" are nearly orthogonal. LEACE is doing exactly what it promises; the lesson is that "we erased gender at block 6" is not a well-formed claim without naming the distribution, and the convenient pooled fit is the one most people reach for.

Erasers fitted on the clean distribution are the wrong projection downstream

In Step 5, erasing at all of blocks 6–11 still left decodability around 0.81 at blocks 7 and up. The reason is visible in how we fitted: every block's eraser was fitted on that block's baseline activations, but once block 6 is erased, block 7 receives a different distribution. Refitting greedily — erase 6, cache 7 with 6 erased, fit 7, erase 6 and 7, cache 8, and so on — fixes the leak.

sequential = {}
for site in SITES:
    current = to_device(sequential) if sequential else None
    acts, _ = collect(train_texts, erasers=current, layers=[site])
    sequential[site] = fit_leace(acts[site].float(), y_train)

pooled_seq, _ = decodability(to_device(sequential), SITES, last_token_too=False)
seq_acc, _ = behaviour(to_device(sequential))
print("sequential LEACE, probe by block:",
      " ".join(f"{l}:{pooled_seq[l]:.3f}" for l in SITES))
print(f"he/she accuracy under the sequential fit: {seq_acc:.3f}")

segments.html:
The sequential fit holds the concept at chance at every block from 6 to 11. Behaviourally it is slightly less destructive than the baseline-distribution fit (he/she 0.674 vs 0.562) — erasing more thoroughly in the linear sense does not monotonically erase more of the behaviour, which is one more reason not to treat decodability and use as the same quantity.

What this notebook does not show

  • Linear only. Everything here removes a linear subspace and is evaluated with linear probes. A nonlinear probe may well recover gender from the erased activations, and the model may retain nonlinear access to it. The behavioural drop is evidence that GPT-2's use of this concept is largely linear at these sites; it is not evidence that no representation remains.
  • One concept, one model, one metric of damage. Gender-of-name on GPT-2 is an easy case: strong, early, and legible at the logits. The same recipe ports unchanged to other decoders — a Llama block's .output is also a bare tensor, so apply_erasure needs no edit at all beyond the module path (model.model.layers) and a dtype match — but the numbers will not.
  • Perplexity is a coarse instrument. +2.9% on 12k tokens of wikitext rules out gross damage, not subtle damage. A capability that matters to you deserves its own eval, the way agreement got one here.
  • "Gender" here is a proxy. We erase what a probe trained on 176 first names calls gender at block 6. That is a statistical direction in GPT-2's residual stream, not the concept as anyone means it, and it should not be read as a debiasing method. Removing a probe's direction is not the same as removing a model's bias — see Gonen & Goldberg, 2019 for what survives this kind of edit.
